5 Recent advancement of machine learning and deep learning in the field of healthcare system

Yogesh Kumar
Chandigarh Engineering College, Landran, Mohali
Manish Mahajan
Chandigarh Engineering College, Landran, Mohali

Abstract

The healthcare sector has long been adapted primarily and significantly from scientific advances. Nowadays, machine learning (ML, a subset of artificial intelligence) plays a vital role in numerous health-related domains, including the expansion of novel medical measures, managing patient information and records, and treatment of chronic ailments. ML in medicine has recently made headlines. Google has developed an ML technique to help recognize cancerous tumors on mammograms. Stanford uses a deep learning method to classify skin cancer diseases. Still, ML advances itself to developments better than other terminologies. Algorithms can deliver instant advantage to disciplines with procedures that are reproducible or consistent. Also, those with huge number of medical image datasets, such as radiology, pathology, and cardiology, are robust aspirants. ML can be qualified to look at images, classify irregularities, and opinion to parts that require attention, thus improving the correctness of all these developments. In future, ML will provide benefits to the family physician at home. ML can also offer an objective opinion to improve productivity, consistency, and accurateness. Healthcare needs to interchange from intelligence of ML as an innovative perception to sight it as a real-world tool that can be organized nowadays. We must take an incremental approach if ML has to play a role in healthcare system. ML has boundless impression in the area of healthcare such as drug discovery applications, robotic surgery, predicting diabetics, liver abnormality, and also in personalized healthcare. The main aim of the chapter is to study the advancement of ML in recent healthcare applications such as automatic treatment or recommendation for different diseases, automatic robotic surgery, drug discovery and development, and other latest domains of the healthcare system. The chapter also comprises the analysis of different ML techniques used in healthcare. Another objective of the chapter provides a systematic procedure to use ML techniques on healthcare domains. The hybrid ML methods can also be used to detect different types of diseases. Using ML algorithms, the efficient system that identifies multicancer diseases can be developed at the same time. The chapter also comprises the analysis based on ML methods and deep learning methods in healthcare system.

Keywords: Machine learning, Deep learning, Cancer disease, Robotic surgery, Classification,

5.1 Introduction

Industrial organizations are using large amount of data that is recognized using machine learning (ML). By collecting perceptions from these data, a more efficient work can be done by organization and can get better results than their competitors (Amin et al., 2013). In various domains, ML algorithms have been used in innovative predictive models (Anand et al., 2015). Even deep learning techniques are used in various day-to-day activities such as advertisement, Google Search, and YouTube. The use of ML and deep learning techniques in the field of multidisciplinary and healthcare informatics has become the same in terms of data handling challenges and technological advertisements (LeCun et al., 2015; Russakovsky, 2015). The scientific field such as health or medical informatics deal with storing, retrieving, and optimal use of medical data as well as information along with a knowledge provided for problem solving and decision making. Over the last few decades, an immense development has been achieved in health technology such as advances in information gathering, communication, research, and treatments. By medical information digitization, there is an increase in patient’s data that can be related to advanced equipment-generated medical results and data provided by patients (Hirschberg et al., 2015). This information revolution is a common outcome, where people face disheartened tasks of interpreting and understanding data. Handling or managing these large amount of data is not possible by simply using manual techniques and tools, and is also a very slow and tedious process. So, to understand the data there is a need of data-driven approaches from computational sciences or data science and data analytics. Critical health information can be extracted, and the medical data can be analyzed using these approaches that can help doctors and patients in making better decisions (Hinton et al., 2012).

Currently for analyzing medical data, a large investment is done in data science by academia and industry. In the coming years, an important role will be played by data science due to rapid growth in the amount of generated data in medicine. Before the deployment of artificial intelligence (AI) systems in healthcare applications, there is a need to train it through clinical activities such as diagnosis, treatment, and screening assessments that generate data (Kotsiantis, 2007). This is done to learn AI by similar groups of subjects and associations between outcomes and features of interest. There are two major categories of AI devices.

First one with ML technique: This will analyze structured data such as genetic, eligible provider (EP) , and imaging data and are used in medical applications that attempt to find the probability of disease outcomes (Brazdil et al., 2003).

Other with natural language processing (NLP): This will extract information from medical journals and clinical notes like unstructured data that supplements and enriches the structured medical data (Cheng et al., 2007). The main target of NLP procedures is to turn texts into machine-readable structured data that is further analyzed using ML techniques.

In this chapter, Section 5.1 provides a brief introduction about the use of ML and deep learning in healthcare; Section 5.2 contains the classification of ML methods that consist of four types. Section 5.3 gives a systematic procedure of using ML techniques in healthcare domains. Section 5.4 gives applications of ML in healthcare that contains work done by various researchers in different areas of healthcare along with the comparative study. Deep learning solutions in healthcare and other industries along with the comparative study are given in Section 5.5, and Section 5.6 contains current and future applications of deep learning in healthcare and medical domain.

5.2 Classification of ML methods

There are large numbers of ML algorithms that are classified into four broad categories on the basis of learning nature (Mishra, 2018). The selection process of ML algorithm consists of features that match the learned data with the existing approach biases. Figure 5.1 shows the types of ML.

5.2.1 Supervised learning

Another name given to supervised learning is the predictive model, which is used for tasks such as use of other values in the dataset including prediction of one value (Anil Mathur, 2007). The process of predictive model training is identified as supervised learning due to a clear instruction given to predictive models about what and how they need to learn. In existence of uncertainty, the supervised ML is able to predict the evidence in existence. Figure 5.2 shows the diagram of speech learning. As in supervised learning algorithms, an output is taken from an input dataset and known data response. Some of the supervised ML algorithms are as follows:

  • Support vector machine (SVM): SVM is considered as the most recent type of supervised ML technique that is closely related to classical multilayer perceptron neural networks (NNs) (Yang et al., 2018). It works on the margin of objects from hyperplane that is drawn for separating two or more than two objects or data classes (Zhang et al., 2012). The expected generalization errors will be reduced by reducing the margin or creating a large distance between the instances and hyperplane separating it.

  • Naïve Bayes (NB): During the stage of classification and training, there is a need of very less storage space in NB supervised ML method (Zhu et al., 2009). That means to store the prior and conditional probabilities, there is a need of very less storage space that results in very less storing memory for training phases but the execution space should be equal to the space of training part.

  • NN: The NN supervised ML methods or techniques are able to perform various tasks of regression and classification but only a single task is performed by an individual network (Hiregoudar et al., 2014). Therefore, in most of the cases there is only single output variable in the network but there can be a number of output units while working on cases having many state classification problems.

  • Decision tree (DT): These trees classify instances by simply sorting them on the basis of values of feature. A feature is represented as an instance to be classified by each node in a DT and an assumed value by each node is represented by each branch in it (Gillies et al., 2012). The classification of instances starts from the root node, and then according to the values of feature, they are sorted out.

  • Bayesian network (BN): It is a graphical model for relationships of probability among various sets of features or any other variable. It is considered as a very famous representative of structured ML algorithms (Shin et al., 2010). As compared to NN or DT supervised ML methods, a most important or different feature of BN is that it considers the possibility of taking prior information about any problem.

5.2.2 Unsupervised learning

Its another name is a descriptive model that is used for tasks that will benefit from understanding summarized data in interesting and new ways. With predictive models, a target of interest is predictive; on the other hand, any feature is a descriptive model that will be more important than any other single feature. Unsupervised learning is the process used for training a descriptive model due to no involvement of learning goal for distinguishing the data and gets few structures (Kaelbling, 1996). It is mainly used on transactional data. Some of the unsupervised ML algorithms are as follows:

  • k-Means clustering: This is a type of unsupervised ML technique that creates groups automatically on initiation of it. Then the items having same characteristics come under the same cluster (Li, 2016). As it creates k distinct clusters according to the input data given to it, this algorithm is known as k-means. In any particular cluster, its mean values are the center of that cluster.

  • Fuzzy c-means

  • Hidden Markov model

They are mainly used to segment text topics and identify data outliers.

Semisupervised learning: It can be used in place of supervised learning. The only difference is to train both labeled and unlabeled data used in semisupervised learning. This type of learning is mostly used in prediction, regression, and classification. And in cases of high labeling cost for a fully labeled training process, a semisupervised learning gives beneficial results (Thompson, 2007). One of the examples in using semisupervised ML algorithm is in recognizing the face of persons on a web.

Reinforcement learning (RL): In this case, a machine is trained to have same decisions in business requirement with the main motive to have maximum efficiency. In it there is less participation of human expertise that results in saving of time. It also helps in discovering the trial and error through algorithms that help in having best rewards. It is most often used in gaming, navigation, and robotics or for decision making. Some of the examples of RL ML algorithms are:

  • Multitask learning: The main motive of multitask learning technique of RL is to help learners so that it can perform in a better way. The procedure of solving any problem is remembered by multitask learning algorithms that help to reach a particular conclusion. After that these steps are used by algorithms that help in finding the similar solution as found while working earlier on the same task or problem. This help is also known as an inductive transfer mechanism in which learners share their experience with each other that helps them all to learn concurrently in a faster way rather than individually (Darcy et al., 2016).

  • Ensemble learning: When a number of individual learners are combined, it is known as ensemble learning. In this case, an individual learner can be a DT, NB, NN, and so on. It has been observed that a better result can be achieved by a collection of learners rather than individual learners (Murff et al., 2011).

  • Q-learning

  • R-learning

  • TD learning

5.3 Systematic procedure to use ML techniques on healthcare domains

Due to storage and generation of large amounts of data, using ML is getting increased in enterprise predictions. In order to have high accuracy and value to enterprise datasets, an effective framework, applications and algorithms, is provided by ML. On the basis of large-scale datasets predictive value, an optimized decision is to find out using ML methodologies. The use of it is effective in handling predictive tasks such as defining behavior that has maximum tendency for driving the preferred outcomes.

5.3.1 Steps to apply ML to data

Below are some of the steps for applying ML task:

  • Data collection

  • Exploring and preparing the data

  • Training a model on the data

  • Evaluating performance of model

  • Improving performance of model

  • Data collection: This is the first block of Figure 5.3. For analysis purpose, data needs to be gathered in an electronic format irrespective of whether it is written on paper, stored in SQL database, and recorded in spreadsheets and text files. According to this gathered data, an algorithm generates an actionable information.

  • Exploring and preparing the data: On the basis of used data quality, an ML project quality is measured. In this step of ML process, there is more involvement of humans. In ML, 80% of effort is dedicated to data, and data exploration is the time spent on learning about data.

  • Training a model on the data: The best algorithm is chosen by ML and then data is represented in the form of model by the chosen algorithm.

  • Evaluating model performance: The estimation performance of algorithm learned from its past experience is very important. Each ML model is able to have a biased solution for each problem related to learning. On the basis of used model test, dataset can be used to evaluate the accuracy of the model.

  • Improve model performance: In order to have a better performance, the performance of each model is enhanced using advanced strategies. There is a need to change the model according to the requirements or to have required results.

After completing these steps, a proposed task is done by deploying a model that is able to achieve acceptable performance. For financial data projection, score data prediction, medical application data, or to automate a task, an ML model is applied. The deployed model failures and successes give the data to train the model for next generation.

5.4 Applications of ML in healthcare

There is a very fast growth in population that makes it challenging to analyze and record a large amount of patient’s data. The healthcare systems become more robust and dynamic with the help of ML that automates the processing and find out data from large database. Medical science and computer science are two types of domains that come in single thread using ML in healthcare. The use of ML techniques helps in advancement of medical science and analyzing the complex medical data for further analysis.

5.4.1 ML in heart disease

Till 2012, an experienced physician judgment was the only way to diagnose coronary heart disease. At that time, current topic was to use computer-intelligent algorithms for coronary heart disease diagnosis in ML. Then coronary heart disease detection was done by Zhang et al. (2012), using statistical learning theory-based SVM. In their work, the test data is classified using classifiers with different kernels along with feature extraction and data preprocessing of original data. They have concluded that radial basis function (RBF) accuracy is highest than all other classifiers. For RBF, an optimization parameter grid search method was used for selecting a best parameter of kernel function and penalty factor. Various researchers have achieved good accuracy in diagnosis of heart disease using artificial neural network (ANN) technique. But still there are some drawbacks of ANN technique such as tuning of number of parameters, activation function must be differentiable, long training process, and obtained solution gets stuck in local minima. Due to all these disadvantages, Fathurachman et al. (2014) have used an extreme learning machine (ELM). The ELM is considered as better generalization model learning algorithm that is faster than DT, SVM, and ANN and also has simple tuning. The results obtained using ELM model shows that it helps in diagnosing heart disease with an accuracy of 83%. Due to involvement of large amount of data, large noise interference, and high data dimension, diagnosis of heart disease is a difficult task that creates a need of using data-driven approaches. So, for diagnosis of heart diseases, Yang et al. (2018) have presented an SVM-based two-dimension–reduction methodologies. For the purpose of diagnosis, more relevant features are achieved using SVM-recursive feature elimination method than for the principle component analysis SVM. The proposed approaches are evaluated, which shows that PCA-SVM is able to achieve 88.24% of classification accuracy via RBF kernel using only size principal components.

5.4.2 Using ML to predict diabetes

As mentioned in the last section, there is rapid advancement in technology and an increase in data that makes a healthcare domain as very important field for researchers. Big data analytics approach has started using in dealing with this large amount of healthcare data. Mir et al. (2018) motive is to propose a WEKA tool using a classifier model that is able to predict the diabetes disease. For analysis purpose, they have used random forest, SVM, simple CART, and NB algorithm. On the basis of efficient results achieved by evaluating each algorithm on the dataset in prediction of diabetes diseases, a best algorithm is find out by them. From performance, it has been observed that in prediction of diabetic disease SVM gives maximum accuracy. As like other diseases, early prediction of diabetes can save human life. Due to this various diabetes-related risk factors are explored by Md. Faruque et al. (2019), using ML techniques as it was able to give efficient results in terms of knowledge extraction. Prediction models are constructed for extracting knowledge from collected diagnostic medical datasets of diabetic patients. This helps in predicting diabetic patients. In their work to predict diabetic mellitus, they have mainly used adult population data such as k-nearest neighbor (k-NN), NB, C4.5 DT, and SVM ML algorithms. On all these four algorithms, an experiment was conducted that shows C4.5 DT with highest accuracy.

Then again in 2019, Alic et al. (2019) have used ML for predicting the future development of type-2 diabetes. For analysis purpose, a San Antonio Heart study data was used and ten features along with SVM were used to build the prediction model. A 10-fold cross-validation was used for training model because in terms of class labels a dataset was unbalanced. In average of 100 iterations, an 81.1% recall rate and an 84.1% of accuracy are achieved that help in identification of the population who was at high risk of developing type-2 diabetes.

5.4.3 ML in prediction of liver abnormalities

The automation is used for prediction of liver abnormalities using ultrasound images. To do it, Hamid et al. (2018) have used ML model for generating normal and abnormal labels and also detect when its prediction is likely to be incorrect. If the proposed model is not able to predict the abnormalities, then it will not generate the label of a test example. The currently used ML models still generate a label for a given example even in the cases of low prediction confidence. Because of it for learning a solver-based novel stochastic gradient decent was proposed by Kanza and then practical, state-of-the-art method was proposed using it. This method was proposed for liver disease classification and then its testing was done using dataset of 100 patients from Pakistan, Multan, and MINAR. To avoid the drawbacks of biopsy, noninvasive ML approaches are used. Hashem et al. (2018) have used a number of ML techniques (genetic algorithm, multilinear regression, particle swarm optimization, and DT) for predicting advanced fibrosis. In this they have combined the clinical information and serum biomarkers for developing a classification model. There were around 40,000 patients who were divided into two sets of prospective cohorts with chronic hepatitis C. To advanced fibrosis age, aspartate transaminase, albumin, and platelet count were found to be significant that has been found by evaluating the proposed model with receiver operating characteristics. The AUROC and HCC achieved while predicting advanced fibrosis in patient is between 0.73 and 0.76, and accuracies achieved using ML algorithms were 66.3% and 84.4%. Vats et al. (2018) have worked on k-means, affinity propagation, and density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise (DBSCAN) ML techniques due to its popularity and good results achieved in the field of data science. It is further compared in terms of computational complexity and prediction accuracy of liver disease prediction in patients. The liver disease-related healthcare dataset was used, and the performance measurement of the above-mentioned three ML algorithms was compared using the Silhouette coefficient. According to this measurement, a k-means is an optimal method in predicting liver diseases.

5.4.4 Automatic robotic surgery using ML

To evaluate disease progression and surgical planning, measuring tissue mechanical properties and localizing tumors have been proved to be useful. Then in artificial tissues, a stiff inclusion mechanical localization was enabled by supervised ML algorithms after automatic robotic palpation. Then for learning algorithms, a training data was generated by Nichols et al. (2019) using specific characterization of elastography and noninvasive and inclusion of tissue biomechanics. A stiffness of artificial tissue was characterized using elastography along with an embedded hard inclusion and after identification of inclusion on the elastography image, the difference in stiffness between surrounding soft tissue and inclusion was identified using ML methods. The stiffness values were labeled using it by being either the part of inclusion or soft tissue. Further through artificial tissues of automatic robotic palpation, a stiffness distributed map was created over the tissue surface. The main motive behind it to find the thresholder against the ML algorithm trained classifiers and label the hard inclusion belonged point theorized. The lack of feedback force was the main limitation of robot-assisted minimally invasive surgeries and by simply adding sensors will not be a practical solution in clinical environment. Due to this, Aviles et al. (2015) have presented a force estimation approach, first, by minimizing an energy functional to reconstruct 3D deformation structure of the tissue surface. Then they have presented the architecture on the basis of recurrent NN-long–short-term memory that gives accurate estimation. The proposed approach is tested that shows a long-term stability is achieved along with a significant improvement in accuracy percentage that ranges from 54% to 78% over existing approaches.

5.4.5 ML in personalized healthcare

A new healthcare approach is personalized healthcare or PH that improves the traditional healthcare system by mainly focusing on Internet of things sensor devices, web-based or social media information, and patient electronic health records collected patients’ data. Then by PH, an AI technique was applied on collected data that helps in improving the clinical intervention, disease progression, prediction of diseases, and patient self-management. Then to make analytic models, ML techniques that were used were integrated into different clinical decision support system and healthcare service applications. From sensor devices, a collected data was analyzed using these models, and behavioral pattern of patients along with their clinical conditions was identified through other sources.

For classification purpose, either supervised or unsupervised ML was used. Sometimes the decisions made by humans can be wrong due to involvement of emotion; on the other hand, computers do not have emotions. So, people are biased in decision making on the basis of their perception toward political, religious, and world. In the available dataset used for training purpose, these factors can create a problem as it was used for training it to make decision. Due to all these factors, the Esurance of dataset that was used for ML becomes challenging. Overcoming these will result in enhancement of personal healthcare. Ahamed et al. (2018) have worked on ML models that were used in recent research and identified its reliability issues and proposed an improvement. For continuous monitoring of everyone health by using biomedical devices and prediction of potential health hazards, a PH plays a crucial role. And if these hazards were not treated on time, then it can become dangerous. Mr. Walinjkar et al. (2017) have mainly focused on constant monitoring of ECG signal of an individual; for this purpose, a 3-lead ECG kit was used and arrhythmia was detected by performing real-time analysis. This enables the prediction of heart risk and at ML phase a classification accuracy was needed to be dealt with as a feature extraction method was developed. This method was able to increase the classification accuracy. For development of prediction models, classification, and learning development, an arrhythmia database (MIT-BIH, Physionet) was used. The proposed models were tested and its results show that an accuracy of 99.4% was achieved using k-NN classifier model along with the cross-entropy error of 7.6 and on test data there was 1.2 of misclassification error.

5.4.6 Discovery of drug prediction using ML

Various researchers have worked on orthogonal technique in which through identification of ligands that are nondockable, search space is reduced using soft computing. This will improve the throughput; on the other hand, the binary classifier can be trained using ML that classifies ligands into dockable and nondockable, the two known classes. Due to it Senanayake et al. (2013) have used random forest, ANN, and SVM ML techniques on single problem domain. The problem domain was a protease receptor of HIV and evaluated its performance that shows an improvement of 90% accuracy in throughput by twofold. They have also proposed and used techniques for construction of training set that proved to be useful for ML in instances of a nonsynthesized receptor. The identification of disease-associated proteins affected candidate molecules is a main problem in drug discovery. Number of ML predictor programs was used for experiment purpose in which new candidates were derived from the chemogenomic projects of Inside Janssen Pharmaceutica. The programs were written in single-node C++ that takes more time in running and are inherently parallel but multiple nodes are not used in it. Harnie et al. (2015) have showed that how pipeline is reimplemented using Apache spark that enables lifting of existing programs into multinode clusters. In spark pipeline benchmark and predictors, no changes were done against the original that helps in linear speedup of up to eight nodes. Along with it, their pipeline was able to generate fewer intermediate files and allow easier monitoring and check pointing.

5.5 Deep learning in healthcare

Another name of deep learning is a hierarchical deep structured learning, which is a division of ML (Hinton, 2006). These AIs emulating inspired algorithms developed a layered hierarchical architecture of learning and data representation. It is also inspired from neocortex in the deep human brain, and layered learning process is able to extract abstractions and features from data automatically. In greedy layer-wise methods when one has to deal with a large amount of unsupervised data and natural learn data representation, then deep learning algorithms give improved results (Bengio, 2009). Deep learning has found its use in various applications like image recognition, biometric, NLP, and medical healthcare. The main motive of this section is to provide the usage of deep learning in various healthcare applications.

5.5.1 Deep learning solutions in healthcare and other industries

Various deep learning patterns and hidden chances were used for treating a patient. From the last few years, a lot of attention has been gained by AI and ML but now even deep learning has created its own path in various fields or industries like tourism, retail, textiles, tourism, and healthcare (Bengio, 2013). The main concern of every person in today’s modern world is their health; that’s why various technologies like deep learning were implemented in health industries. Various ways have been proposed by medical experts for implementation of new technologies that should be able to give good results for better future (Arel, 2010). The deep learning is able to put a large amount of data including patient’s records along with medical reports, insurance reports, and personal data, which help in giving better treatment for a good outcome.

5.5.2 Deep learning in robotic surgery

Due to faster rate of recovery and less pain, laparoscopy is used for minimally invasive surgery in various clinical surgeries. There is very narrow operating space and field of view that is insufficient to tactile feedback that can damage surgical instruments, organs, and tissues. So, during laparoscopic surgery for detection of surgical instruments, a real-time model on the basis of convolutional neural network (CNN) was used Choi et al. (2017). For testing purpose, they have used a dataset of seven surgical tools for learning CNN, then a YOLO unified architecture is used to track surgical instruments in real time. To evaluate a proposed model, a precision and a degree of recall are used for performance that shows an average of 72.26% of accuracy over dataset. It has been predicted that semantic segmentation was a very big problem for robotic instruments surgery in which correct detection of position of instrument was the main challenge for pose tracking and estimation in the vicinity of surgical scenes. In order to address these challenges, there is a need of accurate pixel-wise instrument segmentation; so, for robotic instrument segmentation, Shvets et al. (2018) have proposed a deep learning-based approach that addresses the problem of binary segmentation. Through a feed from surgery video every pixel of images was labeled as instrument or background and also addresses multiclass segmentation problem, in which they had differentiated between different parts and different instruments from the background. The proposed method is tested and compared with other methods for automatic instrument segmentation that gives improvement.

5.5.3 Deep learning in drug discovery

By an increase in drug candidates, there is an increase in social burden of drug discovery. In drug response vitro models, a traditional preclinical drug scene was not able to mimic the complex properties of human biology. Due to this there is need to be contributed. The Gregor Urban et al., has proposed a new micro-physiological system for growing perfused micro-tissues that seems to be suitable for large drug screens and also able to models human physiology accurately. Then in 2018, Gregor U., et al., (2018) have developed a ML model that is able to accurately and quickly predict flag commands that were able to disrupt vascular networks effectively from drug application before and after images in vitro. The proposed system is based on CNN that is able to achieve high or 98.1% of accuracy without putting any false negative effects on system.

In traditional drug discovery, there is problem of cost and time so there is a need to propose a new method that will increase its efficiency. To solve this problem, use of virtual screening (VS) and its database has been a famous method for pharmaceutical research. VS plays a very important role in early stages of drug development and discovery as it helps in reducing the enormous search space of chemical compounds. For effective distinguishing, active and inactive legends are used due to an increase in the count of ligands by time. For big database molecules a screening was done using deep learning algorithms that further classify druglike and nondruglike ligands against a particular protein target. This will result in an increase of VS process speed. Bahi et al. (2018) have proposed a deep NN-based fast compound classification method for VS that is known as DNNVS. Then from a huge database, a Spark-H2O platform was used to label small molecules. The proposed approach that is evaluated shows that the accuracy achieved using DNNVS is 99% and performed well when compared with ML techniques.

5.5.4 Deep learning in disease diagnosis

Breast cancer has become a leading cause of death among women; and for diagnosis and screening of breast cancer, a mammogram is used as a standard. To standardize mammographic reporting, a breast imaging reporting and data system (BI-RADS) lexicon has been developed by the American College of Radiology that enables the decision-making facility of biopsy and assesses cancer risk. Due to the use of inappropriate terms and missing data, unstructured and semistructured free text were made for current biopsy decision making due to variation in their accuracy. Due to BI-RADS lexicon application and occurrence of substantial interobserver variability, a variation takes place that makes critical to incorporate an accurate and novel technique for breast cancer decision-making data. Then to develop an analytic model, He et al. (2017) have combined deep learning methods and NLP that target well-defined and characterized specific breast-suspicious patient subgroups. This model is able to give better results when compared with SVM, Gaussian mixture model, and PCA algorithm. Tourassi (2017) has discussed both theoretical and practical perspectives of the latest deep learning technology that is relevant to clinical pathology NLP reports. Various information extraction tasks of benchmark studies were presented and their importance was discussed in supporting a scalable and comprehensive national cancer surveillance program (Tables 5.1 and 5.2).

5.6 Current and future directions of deep learning in healthcare and medical domains

The current and future applications of deep learning in healthcare are evident and can be easily observed. Some of them are:

  • In healthcare industry, a transfer of knowledge taken from heterogeneous, complex, and high-dimensional biomedical information is a challenging task. In modern world of medical science, there is abundant amount of data like data of sensor text, electronic records, imaging, etch that has been solved to much extension with the use of deep learning algorithms. A complex or unstructured example can be represented successfully with the use of deep learning, and an efficient and new paradigm is obtained using latest deep learning technology that is able to obtain an end-to-end learning model for complex types of data.

  • In advance clinical research, a promising result is obtained using electronic health records and it also better informs the clinical decision-making skills. With modern electronic health records, a predictive modeling can be prevented with a practice of summarizing and representation. The use of alternative feature learning strategy has proved to be successful in patients who have achieved better results using electronic health record data. From various studies done by different researchers, it can be said that use of deep learning framework arguments in clinical environment decision systems gives improved results.

  • In thrombosis, use of urokinase and plasminogen activator streptokinase and therapy can no longer be an approach as approved by the Food and Drug Administration. Instead of it, a deep learning comes into existence for the treatment of acute peripheral arterial thrombosis and embolism along with acute coronary thrombosis.

  • There are some measures and outcomes of deep learning trained algorithms. In detection, a reference diabetic retinopathy sensitive and specificity nature of the algorithm can be defined as worst or moderate one. Because of this reason, two development set-selected operating points are used in deep learning trained algorithms. In this the first operating point handles high specificity and another one handles high sensitivity that results in better results.

  • For identification of relevant information from patient records and charts, a deep learning NN can be used. As a scalable and accurate prediction can be created for variety of clinical resource sceneries, a deep learning approach can be used.

  • It is also been used for analyzing medical images and in future it can also be used in medical segmentation, classification, registration, and various other tasks. Deep learning has been used in medical fields such as neural, digital pathology, pulmonary, and retinal.

  • In predictions, a better result has been achieved using deep learning algorithm developed data. Hence, a very important tool of ML in computer domains such as vision and imaging has been developed.

5.7 Conclusion

A large amount of data has been used by industrial organizations and recognized using ML. By collecting perceptions from these data a more efficient work can be done by organization and gets better results than their competitors. In various domains, a use of ML algorithms has been observed in innovative predictive models. Even deep learning techniques are getting used in various day-to-day activities like advertisements, searching, and YouTube. The use of ML and deep learning techniques in the field of multidisciplinary and healthcare informatics has become the same in terms of data-handling challenges and technological advertisements. There are large numbers of ML algorithms and further they have been classified into four broad categories by considering their nature of learning that is explained in Section 5.2. Supervised learning, unsupervised learning, semisupervised learning, and RL are four ML methods. Section 5.3 includes a systematic procedure to use ML in healthcare. Due to storage and generation of large amounts of data, a use of ML is getting increased in enterprise predictions. In order to have high accuracy and value to enterprise datasets, an effective framework, applications, and algorithms are provided by ML. With rapid growth of population, it becomes challenging to analyze and record the large amount of available data of patients. The healthcare systems become more robust and dynamic with the help of ML that automates the processing and find out data from large database. Medical science and computer science are two domains that come in single thread using ML in healthcare. The use of ML techniques helps in advancement of medical science and analyzing the complex medical data for further analysis. Various researchers have worked on the number of healthcare applications where ML was used. Along with ML, data learning is also being used in medical and healthcare. Another name of deep learning is a hierarchical deep structured learning that is a division of ML. Section 5.4 described deep learning solutions in healthcare and other industries, and a comparison study on work done by various researchers in the field of medical or healthcare using deep learning algorithm. Further, the current and future applications of deep learning in healthcare are evident and can be easily observed as given in Section 5.6.

6 Predicting psychological disorders using machine learning

Prabhsimar Kaur
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, DIT University, Dehradun, India
Vishal Bharti
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, DIT University, Dehradun, India
Srabanti Maji
Department of Computer Science and Engineering, DIT University, Dehradun, India

Abstract

With the world population growing at a rapid pace, a large number of people are getting prone to chronic psychological disorders. The advancements in computer technology and machine learning approach are making healthcare more accessible and affordable for people. Early diagnosis of psychological disorders is also made possible with the aid of machine learning tools, thereby helping in improving a patient’s quality of life. In this section, we have tried to explain the classification of techniques in machine learning – supervised, unsupervised, and semisupervised – and how effectively these techniques are used in psychological disorder prediction. The accuracy levels of each technique have been reported. The recent advancements in machine learning techniques for predicting disorders have been explained. Also the challenges being faced while prediction of psychological disorders have been studied and explained in this chapter.

Keywords: Machine Learning Algorithms, Mental disorder, m-Health, Prediction,

6.1 Introduction

Psychological disorder refers to all of the diagnosable mental disorder patterns in the social & occupational lives; these are psychological systems that have an impact on multiple areas of life. Incidence of mental disorders is rising at a high rate worldwide. According to the World Health Organization, one out of four people will be affected at some point in their lives by psychological or neurological disorders, thus becoming a second major source of global disease till 2020 (Bruce and Edward, 1984). Psychological disorders are becoming most prominent in teenagers and all teens experience some degree of psychological disorders. Half of all the psychological conditions start by the age of 14, yet most cases go undetected and untreated. According to the study reported in WHO, approximately 6.5% of the Indian population is suffering from a serious form of mental disorder with numbers increasing at a rapid pace. Stress is the common mental illness in Europe, affecting about 16% of the total population (Kessler et al., 2016). Psychological disorders are the most ignored and undertreated form of disorders, which lead to immense healthcare and medical costs. Psychological disorders cost around more than $42 billion in the U.S. per annum, while in Europe the cost amounts to 74.4 billion Euros per annum. Psychological disorder is a term often used interchangeably with mental disorders, mental illness, and psychiatric disorders. Mental disorder is a condition that in the unconscious and emotional state of a person is usually characterized by severe disruption. Throughout our social & professional lives, they are generally associated with anxiety and other essential tasks. Mental disorders are the most ignored forms of disorders due to the fear of social stigma that prevents people from getting a proper diagnosis and treatment plan. Mental illness encompasses a wide variety of conditions and is influenced by several factors such as genetics, biology, daily habits, and environment. Every year, one in 25 people experiences severe mental illness, according to the National Institute for Mental Health. (Linthicum et al., 2019).

There may be many forms of mental illness, many types may be classified as psychotic disorders, anxiety disorders, heart control & alcohol disorders, mood disorders, post-traumatic disorders, etc.

6.1.1 This chapter explains how machine learning (ML) is an important technique used to detect mental illness

A paradigm shift in clinical methods and analytical techniques has been generated by the rapid advancement in technology and functional approaches used in medicine, combined with significant advances in computing power, storage, and data collection. ML is the robust technique nowadays that has emerged in the public healthcare sector for early diagnosis of the mental disorder (Kipli et al., 2013). Through the use of technology, clinicians can diagnose and treat mental health problems at a remediable stage, thereby improving the overall wellbeing of the patient. ML can even operate on ambiguous or incomplete knowledge by using principles of probability and pattern matching, e.g., more precise diagnosis, in copying human reasoning and making logical decisions. The quick and shrewd assessment of restorative learning put away in immense databases worldwide would now be accessible to experts to empower them to precisely analyze and treat sickness. This helps eliminate confusion, saves lives, and decreases treatment costs. The growth in the use of ML & Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being welcomed by medical physicians and is providing significant advantages in diagnostics. Computer-based intelligence is discovering more uses in prescription, from the conclusion of psychological wellness to settling on significant clinical choices. Complex psychiatric conditions like schizophrenia and depression are being detected by the professionals using AI, just by talking to the patients. Common mental health issues such as depression, OCD, and anxiety can be identified by voice recognition software and complex data computer analysis. AI is becoming a great tool for psychologists and psychiatrists for accurate diagnosis of specific psychiatric disorders (Luo et al., 2016).

The chapter further illustrates the classification of Machine Learning Techniques and presents a detailed analysis along with accuracy measures and equations of the diseases predicted using these techniques.

6.2 Techniques for machine learning

ML is a subfield of AI that was proposed by Allan Turing and authored by Arthur Samuel in the 1950s (Turing, 2009, pp. 23–65) and has a solid connection with the fields of computer science and measurements (Linthicum et al., 2019). Broadly defined, ML is a computational strategy that learns parameters automatically and methods to find the best solution to the problem with no human intervention for programming. Additionally, ML calculations are ready to develop and change with a new information implementation. Such recognition patterns hold different potential preferences over physically defined models, including effectiveness and unpredictability (El and Murphy, 2015). The year 1990 can be marked as the year when (Provost and Kohavi, 1998) machine learning techniques came into medical use.

ML has certain advantages over the traditional approach that helps in accurate prediction for diseases. Machine learning techniques help to maximize clinical importance and generalizability. Algorithms used in ML accommodate countless variables and at the same time think about exceptionally complex blends among those components. High-dimensional datasets incorporating countless algorithms as potential indicators can be processed through machine learning techniques. ML denotes algorithms that learn from data sets. The inputs of ML algorithms are training sets that comprise both labeled and unlabeled data.

6.2.1 Classification of methods for machine learning

It can be generally divided into three types: supervised, semisupervised, and unsupervised learning techniques (described in Figure 6.1) which vary according to their objectives.

Another type of machine learning technique is the reinforcement learning. This type of machine learning technique focuses on the environmental changes and is not suitable for predicting mental disorders at an advance stage. Thus in this chapter, we shall not be focusing on the reinforcement learning technique.

6.2.2 Disease prediction using supervised machine learning

A. What is supervised learning

It is one of the commonly used technique for disease prediction. Supervised ML can be represented as the search for algorithm from an external source to produce general hypotheses that are used in making predictions for future sources. The output is then presented to “training” data function and is defined by using the algorithm that uses this trained data to map the input variables with the output marked. This way, the algorithm gives the most accurate relation between input and output variable. There is no involvement of humans in supervised learning. Supervised Machine Learning Techniques has two categories as – regression and classification (Kotsilieris et al., 2018). Algorithms designed to predict a number of days a person with cancer may survive is an example of regression problems. Designing algorithms to predict brain cancer is one of the examples of classification problems.

C. Supervised Learning Techniques

Naïve Bayes (NB) is also a supervised ML technique and a numerical method used for classification. It is named after Thomas Bayes who developed the Bayes Theorem. It expects a fundamental probabilistic model and permits to bind uncertainty of it in a moral path after deciding probabilities from the outcomes. So it is used to explain the predictive and diagnostic problems of the process (Murphy, 2006). NB is vigorous to noise in the input dataset. The mathematical representation of the Naïve Bayes classifier is given by equation.

(6.1)${Posterior\, Probability} = P\left( {{Xi}|Y} \right) = \ \frac{P\left( {Y|Xi} \right)P\left( {Xi} \right)}{P\left( Y \right)}$

Where Xi refers to “m” classes whose values are X1, X2, X3, … … .Xm. P(Y|Xi) refers to posterior probability, P(Y|Xi) refers to predictor probability, P(Xi) stand for prior probability and P(Y) stands for predictor probability of the class. The example of Naïve Bayes is shown in Figure 6.2

Support Vector Machine (SVM), most famous supervised ML algorithm introduced in 1995, which can solve both regression and classifications problems (Cortes and Vapnik, 1995). This algorithm draws “hyperplane” and distributes the data within different classes with the goal that all instances that belong to one class get classified on one part and they lie on the opposite part of the plane (shown in Figure 6.3). Linear SVM Classification is characterized for SVM classifying functions, and partitioning happens if the selected line includes the most oppressed portion (Maji and Garg, 2014). For non-linear cases, the advanced selection of kernel and data preprocessing is needed. It has an important application in healthcare as it can predict various diseases from MRI scan reports. The equation for the hyperplane is given below.

(6.2)WT ⋅ x + b= 0

Where b stands for bias value for input variable x and w refers to the weight vector. The SVM classification equation is written using minimization formula as given below.

(6.3)${min}\,_{w,b}\,\left( \frac{w^{T}w}{2} \right)$

Neural Network (NN), also known as the neuron, is an information processing technique that originates from the human mind. This framework incorporates enormous amount of tiny processors that deal with information processing. Various processors used in NN operate as an interconnected system parallel to one another to tackle an issue. NN are known for their capacity approximations, which is why they can be connected to practically any ML issue (Hansen and Salamon, 1990). The result of the NN is defined as

(6.4)$N = \sum_{i = 1}^{H}{v_{i}\sigma\left( z_{i} \right)}$

Where vi refers to ith weight parameter, xi refers to the input vector, wi refers to the weight parameter, σ refers to an sigmoid function, and bi refers to the bias for ith unit. Also zi = wixi + bi and $\sigma = \frac{1}{1 + \ e^{- x}}$ . The structure of NN is presented in Figure 6.4.

k-Nearest Neighbor (kNN) is a kind of object-based learning that depends on similarity with other objects. The objects near others, are known as a “neighbor.” At the point when a new object is placed, distance from every case in the model is determined. By doing this grouping, cases are specified to their most similar nearest neighbor and are put into their groups. The kNN method is also capable of consistently computing the values for the target.

For continuous variables, distance can be calculated using three distance measures, i.e., Euclidean, Manhattan, or Minkowski distance. Whereas for categorical variables, Hamming distance is used. Euclidean and Hamming distances are given in the below equations.

(6.5)${Euclidean\, Distance} = \ \sqrt{\sum\limits_{i = 1}^{k}\left( {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right)2}$
(6.6)${Hamming\, Distance} = \ D_{H =}\sum_{i = 1}^{k}\left| {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right|$

Where i refers to the nearest neighbor whose values are 1, 2, 3 … .k. x and y refer to the variables.

The diagrammatic representation of kNN is given in Figure 6.5 below in which let value of k = 3, so the new data point will lie in class 1 because of the nearest distance.

Decision Tree (DT) also belongs to a class of supervised ML technique. The main aim of DT is to prepare a training model that will help in the predictions of target variables by implementing learning decision rules, which are deduced from training data. Its structure is like a flowchart that consists of leaf nodes, internal nodes, and branches (Figure 6.6). The prediction for any record is always started from the root node. To choose one root variable from a number of variables, one of the methods used is the information gain. Information gain further measures the uncertainty of variable, which is known as Entropy (Safavian and Landgrebe, 1991). The mathematical equation for both Entropy and Information Gain is given below.

(6.7)H = E(S) = ∑I = 1C − pilog2pi

Where pi refers to probability of the ith class.

Random Forest (RF) is another type of supervised ML algorithm introduced by Tin Kam Ho. RF builds the forest like structures with a number of decision trees in which independent vectors are divided equally and individual tree assigns a value 1 (unit) to the most voted input class x (Figure 6.7). More the number of trees in the RF, more accurate will be the prediction (Breiman, 2001). Let h(x|θ1), h(x|θ2), …, h(x|θk) be the number of k classifiers with parameters θk and a random vector θ. Then the equation for the kth decision tree classifier is given by

(6.8)hk(x)  = h(x|θk)

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) algorithm is described as a dimensionality reduction method that is used for pre-processing and pattern classification problems. Its main aim is to reduce the dimensions by transferring the variables from multi-dimensional space to smaller-dimensional space. It is similar to the Principle Component Analysis (PCA) algorithm but works with the labeled data (Zhao et al., 1998). LDA output classification(y) is given by using a discriminant function and illustrated in (Figure 6.8).

(6.9) ${Dk}\left( x \right) = x^{\ast}\left( \frac{muk}{{sig}a^{2}} \right) - \left( \frac{muk}{{sig}a^{2}} \right){+ ln}\left( {Plk} \right)$

Where Dk(x) refers to the discriminant function of class k and the variables Plk, sigma^2, and muk are the variables whose values are calculated from the given data.

Logistic Regression (LR) is another supervised ML technique commonly used in the field of statistics. LR is named after the function called the logistic function (Cook, 1977). To give a binary output (either 0 or 1), the algorithm uses x input values combined linearly with coefficient values. The equation for Logistic Regression is given by:

(6.10)y=e∧(b0 + b1x)/(1+e∧(b0 + b1 * x))

Where the output is denoted by y, b0 refers to the intercept word, b1 refers to the coefficient and x refers to the input variable. The curve for logistic regression is given as in below figure (Figure 6.9).

Gaussian Process is defined as the algorithm which solves both problems of regression and classification. This algorithm is very useful in supervised learning as it can give an estimate of their own uncertainty. It is a stochastic process that works only on a finite set of variables (Rasmussen, 2003). The equation that satisfies the Gaussian process is given as follows.

(6.11)$E\left( {{exp}\left( {i\sum\limits_{l - 1}^{k}s_{l}X_{t_{l}}} \right)} \right) = {exp}\,\left( \left. {- \frac{1}{2}\,\sum\limits_{lj}{\sigma_{l_{j}}s_{l}s_{j + i}\,_{\sum\limits_{l}{\mu_{l}s_{l}}}}} \right) \right.\,$

Where t1, t2, … .., tk are finite variables, μl is the mean of variable, σlj is the covariance with σjj > 0 and s1, s2, … …, sk € R. The curve for Gaussian Process is given in below figure (Figure 6.10).

Ensemble Learning, also known as meta-algorithms merges several machine learning algorithms into one accurate model so as to decrease boosting, bagging, or stacking. This algorithm is basically divided into two categories – sequential ensemble methods and parallel ensemble methods (Dietterich, 2002). Many common types of ensembles are used, such as Bootstrap aggregating, Boosting, Bayes optimal classifier, etc. One of the types of ensemble, i.e., Bayes optimal classifier is expressed by the following equation.

(6.12)y = argmaxcj ∈ C∑hi ∈ HP(cj|hi)P(T|hi)P(hi)

where y is the output label that is being predicted, C is the group of possible outcomes, H is the hypothesis space, P refers to likelihood, and T refers to the data that is used for training. Block diagram of ensemble learning is given in (Figure 6.11).

AdaBoost, also known as Adaptive Boosting is the first boosting algorithm that uses rough and inaccurate rules to produce very high accuracy prediction rules (Rätsch et al., 2001). An AdaBoost algorithm can be combined with other ML algorithms for enhancing their efficiency. It works by combing the output of weaker algorithms into a weighted sum that gives the final accurate output. The mathematical equation for AdaBoost Classification is given as:

(6.13)${F(x)} = {sign}\left( {\sum_{m = 1}^{M}\theta_{mf_{m}(x)}} \right)$

Where F(x) is the correct classifier output which is the weighted M soft classifier combination. Fm is the mth weak classifier and θm refers to the correlating weight. Block diagram of AdaBoost is given in (Figure 6.12).

Gradient Boosting is one of the useful algorithms for building predictive models that can quickly overfit a training dataset. This technique is also named as XGBoost. Gradient Boosting’s main objective deals with combining the prediction strength of all weak algorithms to get more accurate predictive results (Friedman, 2002). The most common type of weak algorithm used in Gradient Boosting is the decision tree. Let Fm be the imperfect model, then a new accurate model equation that uses the h estimator in below equation.

(6.14) Fm + 1(x) = Fm(x) + h(x)

Where h(x) = y − Fm(x) and y is the output variable. The equation for Gradient Boosting using decision tree can be represented in the below figure (Figure 6.13).

6.2.3 Disease prediction using semisupervised machine learning

A. What is semisupervised learning

Semisupervised learnings comprise algorithms that are trained upon a combination of data sets containing both labeled and unlabeled data. Generally, these type of combinations contains small data sets of labeled data and very large data sets of unlabeled data. These algorithms help overcome the basic disadvantages of supervised learning, which involves the hand labeling of data sets either by the machine learning engineer or the data scientists, which is a very costly affair when large sets of data are involved. Also, the application spectrum of unsupervised learning being limited the semisupervised learning algorithms help overcome these disadvantages (Zhu and Goldberg, 2009). Semisupervised learning algorithms’ basic procedure involves clustering of data by the programmer or data scientists using unsupervised learning algorithms and then labeling of rest of the unlabeled data using existing labeled data. The unlabeled data sets are relatively cheap to acquire whereas labeled data sets are very expensive. Semisupervised learning algorithms are based upon certain assumptions, such as continuity assumption, cluster assumption, and manifold assumption.

C. Techniques used for disease prediction in semisupervised machine learning

Genetic Algorithm (GA) is a stochastic search algorithm introduced in 1975 by John Holland for solving optimization problems. GA uses recombination and selection criteria for generating new sample points. They are applied on code that is the finite length of strings called chromosomes. Each string contains a finite length of symbols called genes. New data points are generated by applying further “mutating” and “crossover” process on them. In the medical field, GA is used for classification and feature extraction of high dimensional patterns (Figure 6.14) shows the basic steps for GA.

6.2.4 Disease prediction using unsupervised machine learning

A. What is unsupervised learning

As compared with supervised learning, unsupervised machine learning involves unlabeled data. The primary reason to use unsupervised learning is not to predict target outcome variables; however, to deal with meaningful information without supervision. Some instances where unsupervised learning is used are finding similarities among data objects, figuring out connections among attributes, reshaping attributes to decrease dimensionality, etc. Clustering is a fact finding technique aimed at identifying possible subgroups in the relevant data without previous information from existing groups. For instance, a suicide analyst may want to know which “patients” clusters come from the suicidal pool. (Coates et al., 2011).

C. Techniques used for disease prediction in unsupervised machine learning

K-means clustering algorithm, initially introduced in 1967 by MacQueen (Haraty et al., 2015), is one of the unsupervised ML techniques that can solve the problems of clustering. With each k center, the data set is classified into different k clusters. The result of prediction depends on the distance from the center of clusters so for better results, they should be positioned far apart from each other. Then on the next step, the data set should associate with the nearest center to the belonging cluster. When all points are associated, further re-calculation is done by taking “k” as new centroids. A loop is to be generated by doing this again and again and the k centers will be changing their location on each step. This continues until the changes are no more done. This algorithm’s main objective is to reduce an objective function, also called a square error function which is given in equation (6.15). The K-means clustering example is shown in (Figure 6.15).

(6.15)${Square\, Error\, Function} = J\left( V \right)\ = \sum_{i = 1}^{c}{\sum_{j = 1}^{ci}{\left( \left| \left| {x_{i} - y_{i}} \right| \right| \right)2}}$

Where ||xi – vj|| denotes the Euclidean distance among xi and vj, ci refers to data points in ith cluster and “c” refers to the total number of cluster centers.

Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is an unsupervised learning technique for statistics that is used to find the interrelations between groups of variables. It helps in reducing the dimensions of the dataset by converting a set of correlated variables to uncorrelated variables (Rokhlin and Tygert, 2009). This same procedure is repeated to get a whole new set of variables which are simply known as principle components or orthogonal. PCA is also called as general factor analysis where regression finds a line of best fit. The basic matrix equation for PCA is given by:

(6.16)Y = W′X,

where X is the input matrix with n rows and p columns, Y is the score matrix, and W is the coefficient matrix. The PCA equation is also given in linear form as set of p linear equations:

(6.17)yij = wlixlj + w2ix2j + ⋯ + wpixpj

Let the original dimensions of the dataset be X and Y. By using PCA, the dimension of dataset reduces to new vector Xʹ and Yʹ whole illustration is given in (Figure 6.16).

6.3 Comparative measures for validation of machine learning techniques

So as to assess the prediction rate, there are a few indicators, e.g., precision, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy to evaluate the model’s authenticity. These indicators are determined by confusion matrix given in below figure (Table 6.4). This model is a very useful tool for evaluating the quality of various algorithms for the prediction of diseases (Linden, 2006). The ideal state, which must contain significant data, must be present on the matrix’s main diagonal whereas the remaining values should be marked as zero or non-zero.

Table 6.4:Confusion matrix.

Class A (predicted) Class B (predicted)
Class A
(actual)		 True positive (TP) False negative (FN)
Class B
(actual)		 False positive (FP) True negative (TN)

True Positive (TP) = When observations are positive, and predictions are also “correct.”

False Negative (FN) = When observations are positive, but predictions are “Negative.”

TN = When observations are negative, and predictions are also “Negative.”

FP = When observations are negative, but predictions are “Positive.”

6.3.1 The formulas for various indicators are described below

  1. Accuracy – It is given as the ratio of predictions which are correct, i.e., accurate to the total number of predictions made.

(6.18)${Accuracy =}\frac{\left( {TP + TN} \right)}{\left( {TP + FN + FP + TN} \right)}$

  1. Recall or Sensitivity – It is known as the ratio of positive data points which are actually positive to the sum of all positive data points. It is also referred as TPR that stands for True Positive Rate.

(6.19)${Recall =}\frac{\left( {TP} \right)}{\left( {TP + FN} \right)}$

  1. Precision – It is known as the ratio of predictions correct to the sum of all predictions positive.

(6.20) ${Precision =}\frac{\left( {TP} \right)}{\left( {TP + FP} \right)}$

  1. Specificity – The ratio of positive data points which are actually negative to the sum of all negative data points is known as specificity. It is also referred as FPR that stands for False Positive Rate.

(6.21)${Specificity =}\frac{\left( {TN} \right)}{\left( {FP + TN} \right)}$

Performance comparison of the machine learning techniques for the three random mental disorders like autism spectrum disorder, schizophrenia, and traumatic brain injury have been shown in the (Figure 6.17–6.19) considering 1-Specificity (i.e., FPR) given by x-axis and sensitivity (i.e., TPR) given by y-axis.

6.4 Challenges in machine learning for predicting psychological disorders

Despite significant progress in designing of methodologies that strengthen the importance of ML in medical science applications, some of the challenges still remain, which can be described as follows:

  1. Data availability: The main limitation for using machine learning in predicting mental disorders in advance is the limited size of datasets and their insufficient features description.

  2. Need for traceable conclusions: In real life situations, the doctors are not only concerned about the prediction results given by the ML model. However, they are also concerned about the factors or parameters that led to final prediction. That means for the better treatment of the patient, the doctor needs to know in depth working of the model.

  3. Reproducibility: Prototyping, iterating, and benchmarking machine learning techniques is the another challenge in real life applications. This workflow is a very challenging task when done manually, thus requires computer programming skills for increasing demand.

  4. Simple is better: It is proven that when the data is pre-processed properly, it tends to give more accurate results. But applying feature extraction on a large dataset and ensemble simpler models to make a better predictive model is one of the challenging task while doing predictions using machine learning techniques.

  5. Data management: Datasets gathered from EEG or ECG test is very vast in size that requires proper feature extraction for the implementation of machine learning algorithm. Managing such huge data and separating useful data for research work is another challenging task.

  6. High level of customization required: In real world, health data is in very complex form and the data resources are also limited. Thus, implementation of any ML algorithm on the health data requires high level of customization which is another challenging task for the researchers. The integration of predictive models into the existing healthcare system is also very complex task.

  7. Utilize expertise, not only data: Datasets that are publically available are small in size compared to extensive training that doctors get in medical colleges for their research work. Thus, after so much of advancement in machine learning techniques, still doctors can perform much better that that of any predictive model.

6.5 Conclusion and future work

Through the help of this chapter we can very well conclude that machine learning techniques in areas of mental health are making significant progress and are revealing exciting advances. In this chapter information has been provided about the ML techniques which are frequently used for predicting mental health. We have reviewed around 15 mental disorders that were predicted using three categories of machine learning and the accuracy range for each such diseases using different ML algorithms have been reported. Supervised ML Techniques are mostly used for prediction of mental health diseases, with SVM being the commonly used technique. The data in the mental healthcare domain being sparse, SVM technique provides more accurate predictions. Further we can conclude that unsupervised machine learning techniques are generally less used in the mental healthcare domain in comparison to other techniques. Various challenges which are being faced in areas of ML while analyzing mental disorders have also been described.
